dct_description_sm: The RADARSAT-1 Antarctic Mapping Project (RAMP) was a collaboration between the Canadian Space Agency, NASA (Pathfinder Program and Polar Oceans and Ice Sheets Program), and the US National Science Foundation (Office of Polar Programs) to map the continent of Antarctica using the Canadian RADARSAT-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) in two missions. The RADARSAT-1 C-band SAR, operational from 1995 to 2013, was capable of acquiring high resolution (25 m) images of Earth's surface day or night, under all weather conditions. The first RAMP mission, the Antarctic Mapping Mission 1 (AMM-1), maneuvered the normally right-looking RADARSAT-1 SAR to a left-looking 'Antarctic Mode' to capture the entirety of the continent, providing for the first time a nearly instantaneous, high-resolution view of the entirety of the southern continent and an unprecedented opportunity to finish space-based mapping of one of the few regions of the earth which had been uncharted until that time. The resulting map images provide benchmarks for gauging changes of Antarctica's ice cover and allowed development of the first high-resolution SAR mosaic of Antarctica. Data collection, processing, and initial distribution were completed by the Alaska SAR Facility, Canadian government ground stations at Gatineau and Prince Albert, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and the Vexcel Corporation of Boulder, Colorado. The Ohio State University directed the overall project and scientific activities.
dct_title_s: Antarctica Satellite Mosaics and Tiles from the RADARSAT-1 Antarctic Mapping Project (RAMP) AMM-1, 1997
